l: Comætho, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Comætho was a very beautiful maiden and the priestess of Artemis Triclaria. She loved Melanippus, and they consummated their love in the temple of Artemis and made it their bridal-chamber; the resulting divine anger led to famine, sickness, and human sacrifice.

l: Melanippus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Melanippus was deeply in love with Comætho and surpassed his peers in other respects and in beauty. He and Comætho violated the temple of Artemis Triclaria, after which the country suffered famine, sickness, and increased mortality, and an oracle ordered annual human sacrifices.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Artemis Triclaria had a grove and temple shared by the Ionians of Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis, who celebrated her festival annually through the night. After Comætho and Melanippus made her temple their bridal-chamber, her anger was said to cause famine, sickness, and unusual mortality. The oracle at Delphi ordered the annual sacrifice of the most handsome maiden and lad to her, until Eurypylus brought the chest containing the statue of Dionysus and the sacrifice was stopped.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: A statue of Dionysus was contained in the chest received by Eurypylus son of Euæmon after the capture of Ilium. Its arrival at Aroe was associated with the ending of the human sacrifice to Artemis Triclaria, and the people of Patras honored Dionysus with an annual festival.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Ionians of Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis shared a grove and temple of Artemis Triclaria and kept her festival annually throughout the night. They suffered famine, sickness, and increased mortality after Comætho and Melanippus violated the temple, and they practiced the prescribed annual human sacrifice until Eurypylus arrived.

l: Aroe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Aroe was one of the settlements whose Ionians shared the grove and temple of Artemis Triclaria. Eurypylus was driven by the wind to the sea near Aroe and came ashore there while a lad and maiden were being led to the altar for sacrifice.

l: Patras, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The people of Patras record no Eurypylus other than Eurypylus son of Euæmon. They offer sacrifices to him every year during their festival of Dionysus.

l: Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: After the capture of Ilium, Eurypylus son of Euæmon received a chest containing a statue of Dionysus. Other traditions say that Æneas left the chest behind when he fled Ilium or that Cassandra threw it away as a misfortune to any Greek who found it.

l: the temple of Artemis Triclaria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The temple of Artemis Triclaria was where Comætho and Melanippus satisfied their love and later made their bridal-chamber. Their actions were followed by Artemis’s anger and by the institution of annual human sacrifices.

l: the altar of Artemis Triclaria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: A lad and maiden were being led to the altar of Artemis Triclaria when Eurypylus came ashore near Aroe. This sacrifice revealed to Eurypylus and the local people the place intended by the oracle at Delphi.

l: the river Amilichus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The river near the temple of Artemis Triclaria was called Amilichus, meaning Relentless, during the period when the annual human sacrifice was practiced. It had previously had no name.

l: Milichus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: After Eurypylus arrived and the human sacrifice was stopped, the river was called Milichus, meaning Mild.

l: oracle at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The oracle at Delphi blamed Melanippus and Comætho for the sufferings of the country and ordered annual sacrifices of the most handsome maiden and lad to Artemis Triclaria. It also foretold that a foreign king would bring a foreign god and stop the sacrifice, and it directed Eurypylus to dedicate his chest wherever he found people offering a strange sacrifice.

l: the chest containing the statue of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: After the capture of Ilium, Eurypylus received a chest containing a statue of Dionysus, said by some to have been made by Hephæstus and given by Zeus to Dardanus. Other traditions say that Æneas left it behind or that Cassandra threw it away; when Eurypylus opened it, the sight of its contents drove him out of his mind.

l: the statue of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The statue of Dionysus was inside the chest received by Eurypylus after the capture of Ilium. Seeing it caused Eurypylus to lose his mind, while its arrival with him ultimately coincided with the ending of the human sacrifice to Artemis Triclaria.

l: the annual human sacrifice to Artemis Triclaria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The annual sacrifice of the most handsome maiden and lad was instituted after the oracle at Delphi attributed the country’s famine, sickness, and mortality to Comætho and Melanippus. The sacrifice continued until Eurypylus arrived with the chest containing the statue of Dionysus and was stopped.

l: love, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Love brought Comætho and Melanippus together despite opposition from their parents and led them to violate the temple of Artemis Triclaria. The text says that love can confound human laws and upset honor due to the gods, but that human beings regard love as worth life.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Æsymnetes is the god inside a chest at Patræ, whose worship is overseen by nine men and nine women chosen for their worth. During his festival, the priest takes the chest outside the temple, and the lads of the district perform rites involving crowns of corn, bathing in the Milichus, crowns of ivy, and a visit to his temple. Patræ also contains temples and statues of Artemis, Athene, Apollo, the Dindymene Mother, Zeus, Hera, Nemesis, and Aphrodite, as well as the Odeum and several tombs. The account explains the origins and rituals associated with Artemis Limnatis and describes monuments connected with Preugenes and Patreus.

l: Æsymnetes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Æsymnetes is the god inside the chest. Nine men and nine women, chosen by the people for their worth, look after his worship.

l: the chest containing the statue of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The priest takes the chest outside the temple on one night during the festival.

l: festival of Æsymnetes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: During one night of the festival, the priest takes the chest outside the temple and special rites are performed. The lads of the district go to the Milichus wearing crowns of corn, bathe in the river, put on crowns of ivy, and go to the temple of Æsymnetes.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: In old time, people crowned those being led to sacrifice to Artemis with ears of corn. In the account's present day, the crowns are laid near her statue, and the lads later wear ivy crowns.

l: grove of Laphrian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The grove of Laphrian Artemis contains the temple of Athene called Pan-Achæis.

l: temple of Athene Pan-Achæis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The temple of Athene Pan-Achæis stands inside the grove of Laphrian Artemis. Its statue of the goddess is made of ivory and gold.

l: Mother of the Gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The Dindymene Mother is honoured at Patræ, where her statue is wrought in stone. Attes is also honoured there, although his statue is not shown.

l: temple of the Dindymene Mother, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The temple of the Dindymene Mother stands in the lower part of the city, and Attes is honoured there.

l: market-place of Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The market-place contains a temple of Olympian Zeus, a statue of Athene in the open air, and the tomb of Patreus. Near it are a temple of Hera, a temple of Apollo, an outlet with a gate bearing golden effigies, and the Odeum.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Athene stands beside Olympian Zeus in his temple, and a separate statue of her stands in the open air in the market-place. Her statue in the temple called Pan-Achæis is made of ivory and gold.

l: temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: A temple of Apollo stands in the market-place of Patræ. Near it are a naked bronze statue of Apollo and the tomb of Patreus.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Apollo is represented in a naked brass statue with sandals on his feet, one foot resting on the skull of an ox. The text connects this representation with his association with oxen, citing Alcæus and Homer.

l: statue of Apollo with his foot on an ox skull, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The statue is a naked bronze Apollo wearing sandals, with one foot on the skull of an ox. The account infers that the image reflects Apollo's special association with oxen.

l: Patreus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The tomb of Patreus stands in front of a statue of Athene in the market-place. A gate near the market-place bears a golden effigy of Patreus, and he receives annual funereal rites along with Preugenes at the festival of Artemis Limnatis.

l: Odeum of Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The Odeum stands next to the market-place and contains a notable statue of Apollo made from spoil gained when the people of Patræ alone among the Achæans helped the Ætolians against the Galati. It is more richly beautified than any Odeum in Greece except the one at Athens, which is larger and better equipped; the Athenian Herodes built the latter in memory of his dead wife.

l: Preugenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Preugenes is shown on a gate near the market-place in a golden effigy with Patreus and Atherion. While the Dorians held Lacedæmon and Argos, he obeyed a dream, took the statue of Artemis Limnatis from Sparta, and was assisted by his most trustworthy slave. His tomb stands before the temple of Athene in the precinct of Artemis Limnatis, and he receives annual funereal rites at that goddess's festival.

l: Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Preugenes is said to have taken the statue of Artemis Limnatis from Sparta to Patræ. The goddess is celebrated in a festival during which the old statue is carried from Mesoa to the sacred precincts at Patræ.

l: grove and temple of Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The grove and temple of Artemis Limnatis lie opposite the market-place at an outlet of Patræ. The sacred precinct contains several temples approached by porticoes rather than standing in the open air, including temples of Æsculapius and Athene.

l: statue of Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The statue was taken from Sparta by Preugenes and is generally kept at Mesoa because it was originally taken there. During the festival of Artemis Limnatis, one of the goddess's servants carries the old statue from Mesoa to the sacred precincts at Patræ.

l: festival of Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: At the festival, one of the servants of Artemis Limnatis carries the old statue from Mesoa to the sacred precincts at Patræ. Preugenes and Patreus receive annual funereal rites at the same time.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The unit describes cults, temples, statues, and oracles at Patræ, including those dedicated to Dionysus, Poseidon, Aphrodite, Demeter, Serapis, and Æsculapius. It recounts how Coresus, a priest of Dionysus at Calydon, sacrificed himself to save Callirhoe after Dionysus caused the Calydonians to become insane. It explains that Callirhoe later killed herself, and that a well near Calydon was named after her. It also describes the oracle at Dodona, the healing oracle at Patræ, and local beliefs about Poseidon and other gods.

l: Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Patræ has temples and statues of Dionysus, Poseidon, Aphrodite, Apollo, Demeter, Serapis, and Æsculapius. It has a grove near the sea with a race-course and a well whose water, viewed through a mirror after prayer and incense, gives an oracle about whether a sick person will recover or die. The women at Patræ are twice as numerous as the men, are devoted to Aphrodite, and many earn their living by making hair nets and other dress items from flax grown in Elis.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Dionysus is worshipped at a temple in Patræ under the title Calydonian because his statue was brought from Calydon. At Calydon, he answered the prayer of his priest Coresus by causing the Calydonians to become insane and die, and the oracle at Dodona declared that his wrath caused the affliction. At Patræ, statues of Dionysus called Mesateus, Antheus, and Aroeus are carried to the temple of Æsymnetes during his festival.

l: Calydon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Calydon was once inhabited and had priests of Dionysus, including Coresus. Callirhoe killed herself at a well in Calydon near the harbour, and the well has since been called Callirhoe.

l: Calydonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Calydonians became insane as if drunk after Coresus appealed to Dionysus, and they died beside themselves. They consulted the oracle at Dodona and learned that Dionysus's wrath would continue until Callirhoe or a volunteer was sacrificed.

l: Coresus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Coresus was a Calydonian priest of Dionysus who loved Callirhoe, although she disliked him. After Dionysus afflicted the Calydonians, Coresus served as the sacrificial priest but killed himself instead of Callirhoe, yielding to love rather than anger.

l: Callirhoe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Callirhoe was the maiden loved by Coresus, but she did not return his love. She was chosen as the victim required to end the Calydonians' affliction, and after Coresus died in her place, she repented and killed herself at a well near the harbour of Calydon.

l: insanity of the Calydonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The insanity of the Calydonians was caused by Dionysus after Coresus prayed to him. The Calydonians became insane as if drunk and died beside themselves, and the oracle at Dodona said the condition would not end until Callirhoe or another volunteer was sacrificed.

l: death of the Calydonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Calydonians died beside themselves after Dionysus caused them to become insane. Their deaths led them to consult the oracle at Dodona about the cause and remedy of the affliction.

l: Dodona, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Dodona was consulted by the Calydonians because the Ætolians, Acarnanians, Epirotes, and other inhabitants of the mainland believed in its oracular responses from doves and the oak.

l: oracle at Dodona, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The oracle at Dodona declared that Dionysus's wrath had caused the Calydonians' trouble. It said that the trouble would not end until Coresus sacrificed Callirhoe or someone volunteered to die instead of her.

l: sacrifice of Callirhoe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The sacrifice of Callirhoe was prescribed by the oracle at Dodona as a means of ending Dionysus's wrath and the Calydonians' affliction. After the required preliminary rites, Callirhoe was led to the altar, but Coresus killed himself in her place.

l: self-sacrifice of Coresus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The self-sacrifice of Coresus occurred when he served as priest at the altar and killed himself instead of Callirhoe. He acted from love rather than anger, and Callirhoe repented after seeing him dead.

l: suicide of Callirhoe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Callirhoe's suicide followed Coresus's death in her place. Moved by pity and shame at his fate, she cut her own throat at a well in Calydon, which was thereafter called Callirhoe.

l: Poseidon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Poseidon has a temple near the harbour at Patræ and an erect statue made of white stone. His universal titles include Pelagæus, Asphalius, and Hippius; he is probably called Hippius because he was believed to have invented riding. Pamphus calls him the giver of horses and ships with sails.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Aphrodite has temples at Patræ, including a sacred enclosure near the harbour and a temple in the grove near the sea. One of her statues was fished up by fishermen, while another is made of wood except for its stone fingers, toes, and head. The women of Patræ are described as especially devoted to her.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Pharæ is an inland town of Achaia reckoned with Patræ since the time of Augustus, with a market-place containing a statue and oracle of Hermes. The people of Pharæ venerate Hermes’ well, its sacred fish, and thirty square stones associated with different gods, and they maintain groves and altars for Castor and Pollux. Tritea is another inland town reckoned with Patræ, known for a painted tomb, temples to the Greatest Gods and Athene, and traditions about its foundation. The coast between Patræ and Ægium includes Rhium, Panormus, the wall of Athene, Erineus, and several rivers and sanctuaries.

l: Pharæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Pharæ is a town in Achaia reckoned with Patræ since the days of Augustus. It lies about 150 stades from Patræ and about 70 stades from the sea, near the river Pierus, and has a large market-place, Hermes’ well, sacred stones, and a grove of Castor and Pollux nearby. Its founder is uncertain: some associate it with Phares, son of Phylodamia, while others suggest someone of the same name.

l: Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Patræ is the town with which Pharæ and Tritea are reckoned by Imperial order. Pharæ is about 150 stades from Patræ, while the promontory of Rhium is about 50 stades from Patræ and the river Milichus and temple of Triclaria are not far from it.

l: market-place of Pharæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The market-place of Pharæ is large according to ancient custom. In its middle stands the statue of Hermes of the Market-place, beside a hearth used for sacrifices and consultation of the oracle.

l: Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Hermes is honored at Pharæ through a statue, an oracle, a sacred well, and thirty square stones near the statue that are each named for one of the gods. The fish in Hermes’ well are not caught because they are considered sacred to him.

l: statue of Hermes of the Market-place, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The statue is a small, bearded, square stone figure lying on the ground in the market-place of Pharæ. An inscription identifies it as an offering of the Messenian Simylus, and it is called Hermes of the Market-place.

l: oracle of Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: A person consulting the oracle at evening burns frankincense on the hearth, fills and lights the brazen lamps, places a brass coin on the altar to the right of the statue, and whispers a question into the statue’s ear. The person then leaves, stops up the ears, and treats the next thing heard after removing the hands as the oracular response.

l: Tritea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Tritea is an inland town of Achaia reckoned with Patræ by Imperial order and lying about 120 stades from Pharæ. It has a temple to the Greatest Gods with clay statues, a temple and stone statue of Athene, and traditions that its founder was either Celbidas of Cumæ or Melanippus, son of Ares and Tritea. The people of Tritea sacrifice to both Ares and Tritea, and the old statue of Athene was said to have been taken to Rome.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The account describes the ruins of Argyra, the rivers Selemnus and Bolinæus, and traditions about their origins and powers. Selemnus was said to have been a handsome shepherd loved by the sea-nymph Argyra, until Aphrodite transformed him into a river and granted him forgetfulness of her. At Ægium, the narrator describes temples and statues of Ilithyia, Æsculapius, Athene, Hera, Dionysus, Zeus Soter, and the Argive gods. He also records a dispute with a Sidonian about whether Æsculapius represented health-giving air and whether Apollo was his father.

l: Selemnus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Selemnus is a river flowing into the sea near Argyra. The local tradition says that Aphrodite transformed Selemnus, who was dying for love of Argyra, into a river and later granted him forgetfulness of her; its water was also said to cure love.

l: Selemnus (handsome youth), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Selemnus was said to have been a handsome youth who fed his flocks near Argyra. The sea-nymph Argyra loved him and slept with him, but stopped visiting after he lost his good looks.

l: Argyra (sea-nymph), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Argyra was said to have been a sea-nymph who came up from the sea to sleep with Selemnus because she was enamoured of him. She later ceased visiting him when he lost his good looks.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Aphrodite transformed the love-stricken Selemnus into a river after he was deprived of Argyra. She eventually granted him forgetfulness of Argyra.

l: love-cure, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The water of the Selemnus was traditionally believed to cure love in both men and women by making those who bathed in it forget their love. The narrator says that, if the tradition were true, the water would be more valuable than great wealth.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Apollo was said to have been enamoured of a maiden called Bolina, who fled from him by throwing herself into the sea. In a dispute at Ægium, a Sidonian identified Apollo with the Sun and called him the father of Æsculapius.

l: Ægium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Ægium had temples to Ilithyia, Athene, and Hera, a temple and statue of beardless Dionysus, and sacred precincts of Zeus Soter. It also contained a sacred enclosure of Æsculapius, a portico for the athlete Strato, and statues called the Argive gods.

l: temple of Ilithyia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The temple of Ilithyia at Ægium contained an ancient statue of Ilithyia. The statue was made by the Messenian Damophon and was veiled except for its face, fingers, and toes, which were of Pentelican marble.

l: Ilithyia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Ilithyia's statue at Ægium held a torch in one hand while the other hand was stretched out straight. The narrator suggests that the torches may symbolize the fiery pains of childbirth or Ilithyia's bringing children to the light.

l: Damophon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Damophon, identified as a Messenian, made the statue of Ilithyia at Ægium. An iambic inscription also attributes the statues of Hygiea and Æsculapius in the nearby sacred enclosure to him.

l: sacred enclosure of Æsculapius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The sacred enclosure of Æsculapius was near the temple of Ilithyia at Ægium. It contained statues of Hygiea and Æsculapius, both attributed by an inscription to Damophon.

l: Æsculapius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Æsculapius had a sacred enclosure and statues at Ægium. A Sidonian said that Æsculapius was the health-giving air rather than the child of a mortal woman, while the narrator noted that a statue of Æsculapius at Titane was called Health.

l: Phœnicians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: A Sidonian claimed that the Phœnicians had more accurate general knowledge about divine matters than the Greeks. The Phœnician tradition he reported made Apollo the father of Æsculapius and interpreted Apollo as the Sun.

l: health, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Health was associated with Æsculapius at Titane, where his statue was called Health. The narrator also accepted the view that the Sun's course produces health among mankind and that the Sun regulates the seasons and gives health to the air.

l: Argive gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: At Ægium, brazen statues of Poseidon, Hercules, Zeus, and Athene were called the Argive gods. The Argive tradition said they had been made at Argos, while the people of Ægium said the Argives had deposited them there; the statues remained at Ægium after the Argives could not repay the sacrifices made for them.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Ægium contains temples and statues honoring several gods, including Zeus Homagyrius, and remains the site of the general meeting of the Achæans. Helice, once an important city with a holy temple of Poseidon of Helice, was destroyed after the Achæans drove suppliants from the temple and killed them. An earthquake and simultaneous sea inundation overwhelmed Helice, leaving its ruins difficult to see beneath or near the sea. The text also describes signs preceding earthquakes and distinguishes several kinds by their effects.

l: Ægium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Ægium has temples to Apollo, Artemis, Aphrodite, Poseidon, Proserpine, Zeus Homagyrius, Pan-Achæan Demeter, and Safety, as well as statues of several gods. It is still the place where the general meeting of the Achæans is held.

l: Poseidon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Poseidon has a temple near the sea at Ægium. He is said to have quickly punished the Achæans after they drove suppliants from the temple at Helice and killed them, sending an earthquake that destroyed the city.

l: Zeus Homagyrius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Zeus Homagyrius, meaning the Gatherer, has a temple and statues at Ægium. He received this surname because Agamemnon gathered the most famous men in Greece there to deliberate together about attacking the realm of Priam.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Achæans held their general meeting at Ægium. At Helice, they drove suppliants from Poseidon of Helice's temple and killed them, after which an earthquake and sea inundation destroyed the city.

l: Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Helice was once an important city about 40 stades from Ægium and contained the most holy temple of Poseidon of Helice. An earthquake and simultaneous encroachment of the sea overwhelmed the city, and its ruins later became difficult to find and less clearly visible.

l: Poseidon of Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Poseidon of Helice had his most holy temple at Helice, and his worship continued among the Ionians after they were driven away. Altars and precincts dedicated to him also existed at Miletus and Teos.

l: destruction of Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The earthquake that destroyed Helice was described as the most deadly kind, undermining the foundations of buildings and making them rock to and fro. It left no clear trace of previous habitation and, together with the sea's advance, rased Helice to the ground.

l: sea inundation of Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The sea encroached over much of the district in winter and completely flooded Helice. It submerged the grove of Poseidon so that only the tops of the trees remained visible and helped sweep away the city and its population.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The unit describes the punishment said to follow outrages against suppliants, citing Dodona, the Areopagus, the Eumenides, the Lacedæmonians, and the Athenians. It recounts the destruction of Helice during the archonship of Asteus and the subsequent occupation of its territory by the people of Ægium. It then describes Cerynea, including its connection with refugees from Mycenæ and its temple of the Eumenides, followed by accounts of Bura, the Buraicus oracle of Hercules, the river Crathis, and the nearby sanctuary of Earth.

l: Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Helice was totally destroyed by the god, and none of its people remained afterward. Its territory was occupied by the people of Ægium. The unit also says that Helice had formerly received gifts for Poseidon.

l: vengeance of heaven for outrages upon suppliants, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The unit presents heavenly vengeance for outrages against suppliants as certain. It associates this vengeance with the destruction of Helice, the earthquake at Lacedæmon, and the punishment of those who destroyed suppliants of Athene.

l: Dodona, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Dodona was the place from which Zeus gave the Athenians an exhortation to respect suppliants. Its message instructed them to treat conquered Lacedæmonians as suppliants and not to kill or harm them.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Zeus at Dodona warned the Athenians to remember the Areopagus and the smoking altars of the Eumenides. He instructed them to treat the Lacedæmonians conquered in battle as inviolable suppliants.

l: oracle at Dodona, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The oracle at Dodona delivered a message to the Athenians in the days of Aphidas. It commanded them to spare conquered Lacedæmonians who sought protection as suppliants.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Athenians remembered the message from Dodona when some Lacedæmonians fled to the Areopagus and the altars of the August after Codrus died. They allowed those suppliants to depart safely, although later authorities destroyed the suppliants of Athene who had occupied the Acropolis.

l: Areopagus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Areopagus was invoked in the message from Dodona as a reminder of the consequences of violating suppliants. Some Lacedæmonians fled there for safety after their army withdrew from Attica.

l: Eumenides, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Eumenides had smoking altars at the Areopagus, and the altars of the goddesses called the August served as a refuge for Lacedæmonian suppliants. Cerynea also had a temple dedicated to them.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Some Lacedæmonians entered Athens by night during the reign of Codrus, then fled to the Areopagus and the altars of the August when their army withdrew. The Athenians allowed these suppliants to leave safely. Earlier, Lacedæmonians who killed suppliants in the temple of Poseidon at Tænarum were followed by a long and violent earthquake.

l: suppliants, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Suppliants are described as inviolable, and the message from Dodona forbade killing or harming them. The Athenians spared Lacedæmonian suppliants on one occasion, while those who destroyed the suppliants of Athene were considered accursed by the goddess.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Athens was the city whose people received the warning from Zeus at Dodona. During the reign of Codrus, Lacedæmonians entered Athens by night, but some fled to the Areopagus when the Athenians began to muster against them.

l: Peloponnesians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Peloponnesians came to Athens during the reign of Codrus son of Melanthus. Most of their army withdrew from Attica after hearing of Codrus’s death and the circumstances surrounding it.

l: Codrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Codrus, the son of Melanthus, was king when the Peloponnesians came to Athens. He devoted himself in accordance with the oracle at Delphi, and after his death the Peloponnesians no longer expected victory.

l: oracle at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The oracle at Delphi was followed by Codrus, who devoted himself in accordance with its message. His death caused the Peloponnesians to withdraw from Attica.

l: destruction of Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The destruction of Helice occurred when Asteus was Archon at Athens, in the fourth year of the 101st Olympiad, when Damon of Thuria was victor. No inhabitants remained afterward, and the people of Ægium occupied the territory.

l: Cerynea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Cerynea was a town built on a hill above the high-road, named either for a local ruler or for the river Cerynites. It became more powerful after receiving more than half of the people of Mycenæ and was later notable for its temple of the Eumenides.

l: Mycenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Mycenæ could not be captured by the Argives because of the strength of its fort, which had been built by the Cyclopes. Its people were forced to evacuate when their supplies failed.

l: people of Mycenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: After evacuating Mycenæ, some of its people went to Cleonæ, more than half took refuge with Alexander in Macedonia, and the rest went to Cerynea. Their arrival made Cerynea more powerful and later more notable.

l: temple of the Eumenides at Cerynea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The temple of the Eumenides at Cerynea was said to have been built by Orestes. Anyone stained with blood or another defilement who entered to look around was immediately driven frantic by fear, so admission was not granted indiscriminately.

l: Bura, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Bura was a town on a hill, said to have been named for Bura, the daughter of Ion and Helice. It suffered a mighty earthquake when Helice was destroyed, and none of its old temple statues survived. Its temples included those of Demeter, Aphrodite, Dionysus, Ilithyia, and Isis.

l: Crathis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Crathis was a perennial river that flowed into the sea and rose in an Arcadian mountain of the same name. The river near Croton in Italy was said to have received its name from this Crathis. The former town of Ægæ lay near it.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Ægira, formerly called Hyperesia, is described through its temples, statues, origin story, and surrounding roads and settlements. The Hyperesians used torches fastened to goats’ horns to deter an invasion by the Sicyonians, and afterward associated their city’s new name with the goats and Artemis the Huntress. Phelloe lies inland from Ægira, while Pellene is the neighboring Achaean town and Aristonautæ its seaport. The unit also discusses Donussa, a town subject to Sicyon, and competing traditions about local names and origins.

l: Ægira, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Ægira is both a town and a seaport, with the seaport 72 stades from the temple of Hercules Buraicus and the upper town 12 stades from the port. It contains temples and statues of Zeus, Artemis, Apollo, Æsculapius, Serapis, Isis, Celestial Aphrodite, and the Syrian goddess, as well as a building with statues of Fortune, Cupid, and a grieving family group. A road from Ægira leads about 40 stades over the mountains to Phelloe, and the seaport of Pellene, Aristonautæ, is 120 stades away by sea.

l: Hyperesia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Hyperesia was the former name of Ægira, and it is the name used for the town in Homer. Its people, fearing an invasion by the Sicyonians, fastened torches to goats’ horns to make the enemy think allied forces were approaching, after which the town’s name was changed.

l: Sicyonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Sicyonians planned to invade the land of the Hyperesians. They withdrew after mistaking torches fastened to goats’ horns for the campfires of allied troops, and they later destroyed Donussa.

l: goats of Ægira, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The goats of Ægira were gathered by the Hyperesians, who fastened lit torches to their horns to frighten the Sicyonians. The most handsome goat, described as the leader of the others, crouched at a place where the Hyperesians later built a temple to Artemis the Huntress.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Artemis the Huntress was credited by the Hyperesians with inspiring their stratagem against the Sicyonians. A temple was built where the leading goat had crouched, and another temple to Artemis the Huntress stood along the road from Ægira toward its seaport.

l: Iphigenia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Iphigenia, the daughter of Agamemnon, was identified by the people of Ægira with an old statue standing in the temple of Artemis. If their tradition was correct, the temple had originally been built for Iphigenia.

l: Sicyon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Sicyon had authority over Donussa, which was described as a town subject to Sicyon. The Sicyonians associated with Sicyon invaded the land of the Hyperesians and later destroyed Donussa.

l: Phelloe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Phelloe lies about 40 stades from Ægira by a hilly road over the mountains. It was not very important and was uninhabited when the Ionians occupied the land, but its neighborhood was suitable for vines, wildlife, and abundant water. Phelloe had temples to Dionysus and Artemis.

l: Pellene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Pellene is next to Ægira and is the last of the Achaean towns near Sicyon and Argolis. Its people said that it was named after Pallas, one of the Titans, while the Argives attributed the name to the Argive Pellen. Pellene’s seaport was called Aristonautæ.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Achæans are associated with the boundary near Pellene, whose people are described as the last of the Achæans near Sicyon and Argolis. A man from Ægira was said to have died fighting most bravely against the Achæans.

l: Aristonautæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Aristonautæ was the seaport of Pellene. It was said to have received its name because the Argonauts put in at its harbor, and it lay 120 stades from Ægira by sea and half that distance from Pellene.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Pellene is a town built on the more level parts of a steep hill, with numerous temples, shrines, a gymnasium, and civic structures. Its religious sites include those dedicated to Hermes, Athene, Artemis, Dionysus, Apollo Theoxenius, Ilithyia, Poseidon, and Mysian Demeter at nearby Mysæum. Promachus of Pellene is honored for his athletic victories and military deeds, while Chæron is neglected because he helped establish tyranny in Pellene. Nearby sites include Mysæum, the healing temple of Æsculapius called Cyros, and the rivers Crius and Sythas.

l: Pellene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Pellene is built on the more level parts of a steep hill whose precipitous peak divides the town into two sections. It contains temples and sacred places dedicated to Hermes, Athene, Artemis, Dionysus, Apollo Theoxenius, Ilithyia, and Poseidon, as well as a market-place conduit, an old gymnasium, and civic rules requiring prospective citizens to reach manhood before enrollment. The people of Pellene honor Promachus highly, but do not care to mention Chæron because he accepted a large bribe from Alexander the son of Philip to become tyrant of Pellene.

l: Promachus of Pellene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Promachus of Pellene, the son of Dryon, won one pancratium victory at Olympia, three at the Isthmus, and two at Nemea. The people of Pellene erected statues of him at Olympia and in the gymnasium, and he is said to have killed most of the enemy facing him in the war between Corinth and Pellene. He is also said to have defeated Polydamas of Scotussa at Olympia, though the Thessalians dispute this.

l: Mysæum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Mysæum lies about 60 stades from Pellene and contains the temple of Mysian Demeter, which was said to have been built by Mysius of Argos. Its seven-day festival includes a night when men, male dogs, and other males are excluded while women perform the customary rites; when the men return, the women and men jest and banter with one another. The site has a grove of many kinds of trees and abundant springs.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK VIII.--ARCADIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Arcadia is described as the inland division of the Peloponnese, inhabited near Argolis by the people of Tegea and Mantinea and shut off entirely from the sea. The Arcadians say that Pelasgus was their first settler and that he became their king. Pelasgus introduced huts, garments made from pig hides, and guidance about which plants and fruits were safe to eat, especially acorns. During his reign, Arcadia was said to be called Pelasgia.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK VIII.--ARCADIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Arcadia is an inland region of the Peloponnese, inhabited near Argolis by the people of Tegea and Mantinea along with other Arcadians. It is entirely shut off from the sea, so Homer describes the Arcadians as going to Troy in transports provided by Agamemnon. The Arcadians say that the region was first settled by Pelasgus and was called Pelasgia during his reign.

l: Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK VIII.--ARCADIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Peloponnese is described as having coastal states including Corinth, Epidaurus, Trœzen, Hermion, Lacedæmonian territory, Messenia, Sicyon, Achaia, and Elis. Arcadia forms its inland division and has no access to the sea.

l: Pelasgus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK VIII.--ARCADIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Pelasgus is said by the Arcadians to have been the first settler of their land and became their king because of his strength, beauty, and judgment. He introduced huts, garments made from pig hides, and instruction about edible plants and fruits, especially acorns. During his reign, Arcadia was said to have been called Pelasgia.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Lycaon, son of Pelasgus, founded Lycosura on Mount Lycæus, called Zeus Lycæus, and established the festival called the Lycæa. Unlike Cecrops, who offered cakes and sacrificed nothing living, Lycaon sacrificed a baby to Zeus Lycæus and was said to become a wolf. The account presents this transformation as an old and credible Arcadian tradition, while also reporting that later wolf transformations could be reversed after ten months without eating meat. Niobe was likewise said to have become a stone and to weep on Mount Sipylus.

l: Lycaon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Lycaon, the son of Pelasgus, founded Lycosura on Mount Lycæus, called Zeus Lycæus, and established the Lycæa. He sacrificed a baby on the altar of Zeus Lycæus and was said to become a wolf afterward.

l: Lycosura, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Lycosura was founded by Lycaon on Mount Lycæus.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Zeus Lycæus was the deity whom Lycaon called by that name and to whom he established the Lycæa. Lycaon sacrificed a baby on his altar.

l: Lycæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Lycæa was a festival established by Lycaon for Zeus Lycæus.

l: Cecrops, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Cecrops, king of Athens, was thought to be a contemporary of Lycaon. He was the first to call Zeus supreme and offered national cakes called pelani instead of sacrificing anything living.

l: wolf transformation, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Lycaon was said to have become a wolf immediately after sacrificing a baby to Zeus Lycæus. A later tradition held that a person transformed into a wolf at the Lycæa could become human again after abstaining from meat for ten months, but would remain a beast if he tasted meat.

l: gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The gods were said in earlier times to receive righteous and pious men at their tables, honor the good, and show wrath toward the wicked. Some gods of that period had been mortals who continued to be worshipped, including Aristæus, Britomartis, Hercules, Amphiaraus, Castor, and Pollux.

l: Niobe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus, was said to have become a stone. She was also said to weep on Mount Sipylus during summer.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The third generation after Pelasgus expanded Arcadia in population and cities, as the sons of Lycaon founded numerous towns. Nyctimus, Lycaon’s eldest son, succeeded to his power, while Œnotrus received money and men from him and sailed to Italy, becoming king of Œnotria. Œnotrus’s voyage was described as the first colony to depart from Greece. Lycaon’s daughter Callisto was associated with Zeus, transformed into a she-bear by Hera, and placed among the stars as the Great Bear.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Arcadia advanced in population and cities in the third generation after Pelasgus. The sons of Lycaon founded many cities in Arcadia.

l: Lycaon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Lycaon was the father of Nyctimus, Œnotrus, and many other sons, as well as his only daughter, Callisto.

l: Nyctimus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Nyctimus was the eldest son of Lycaon and succeeded to all his power. He gave money and men to his brother Œnotrus, enabling Œnotrus to sail to Italy.

l: Œnotrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Œnotrus was the youngest son of Lycaon. With money and men from Nyctimus, he sailed to Italy and became king of the country called Œnotria.

l: Œnotria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Œnotria was the country in Italy that was called after Œnotrus, who became its king.

l: colonization, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Œnotrus’s voyage to Italy was described as the first colony to depart from Greece. The text states that no foreign voyages for colonization had occurred before it.

l: Callisto, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Callisto was Lycaon’s only daughter. After Zeus had an intrigue with her, Hera turned her into a she-bear, and Artemis shot her to please Hera; Callisto was then associated with the constellation called the Great Bear, although the Arcadians showed her grave.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Zeus had an intrigue with Callisto. He sent Hermes to save the child with which Callisto was pregnant and turned the child into the constellation known as the Great Bear.

l: Great Bear, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Great Bear was the constellation into which Zeus turned the child of Callisto. Homer mentioned it in the account of Odysseus’s voyage from Calypso, and it may have received its name in honor of Callisto.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: After Nyctimus died, Arcas succeeded him as king, introduced agriculture and crafts, and changed the names Pelasgia and Pelasgi to Arcadia and Arcadians. Arcas had three legitimate sons by the Dryad Nymph Erato and divided the country among them, while his descendants founded cities and gave their names to regions and landmarks. The kingdom later passed to Aleus, who built the temple of Athene Alea at Tegea and had four children, including Lycurgus. Lycurgus became king as the eldest son of Aleus, killed Areithous by guile, and outlived both of his sons.

l: Arcas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Arcas succeeded Nyctimus as king and introduced sowing corn, breadmaking, weaving, and spinning to his people. He mated with the Dryad Nymph Erato and had Azan, Aphidas, and Elatus by her, as well as an earlier bastard son, Autolaus. When his legitimate sons grew up, he divided the country among them.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: During Arcas’s reign, the country was called Arcadia instead of Pelasgia. After Clitor died without children, its kingdom devolved upon Æpytus and later passed to Aleus.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: During Arcas’s reign, the inhabitants were called Arcadians instead of Pelasgi. Arcas taught his people agriculture, breadmaking, weaving, and spinning.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Tegea and the neighbouring country were given to Aphidas, so poets called Tegea the lot of Aphidas. Aleus later built the old temple to Athene Alea at Tegea and made it the seat of his kingdom.

l: Aleus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Aleus inherited Aphidas’s share and succeeded Æpytus as king because he was his grandson. He built the old temple to Athene Alea at Tegea and had three sons, Lycurgus, Amphidamas, and Cepheus, and one daughter, Auge.

l: Lycurgus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Lycurgus succeeded his father Aleus as king by virtue of being the eldest son. He slew Areithous by guile rather than fairly, and he survived both of his sons, Epochus and Ancæus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The unit traces the succession of Arcadian kings from Echemus through the descendants of Cypselus and recounts their relations with the Dorians, Lacedæmonians, and Messenians. Agapenor led the Arcadians to Ilium, was carried to Cyprus after its capture, and founded Paphos, while later rulers transferred the royal seat from Tegea to Trapezus and faced conflicts with Lacedæmon. The Arcadians supported Aristodemus and the Messenians in their war against the Lacedæmonians. Aristocrates committed sacrilege against Artemis Hymnia, and his descendant Aristocrates later betrayed the Messenians at the Great Trench; this led to the deposition of all the descendants of Cypselus from the Arcadian sovereignty.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Arcadians were ruled by Echemus, Agapenor, and a succession of later kings. They supported the Messenians against the Lacedæmonians, stoned Aristocrates to death for defiling the sanctuary of Artemis Hymnia, and later stoned another Aristocrates for accepting Lacedæmonian bribes and betraying the Messenians.

l: Dorians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Dorians, led by Hyllus, attempted to return to the Peloponnese but were defeated by the Achæans near the Isthmus of Corinth, and Echemus killed Hyllus in single combat. Three generations later they returned by ship and landed near the Promontory of Rhium.

l: Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Dorians under Hyllus attempted to enter the Peloponnese by way of the Isthmus of Corinth but were defeated. Their later return was made by sea, with a landing near the Promontory of Rhium.

l: Agapenor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Agapenor, son of Ancæus and grandson of Lycurgus, succeeded Echemus and led the Arcadians to Ilium. After Ilium was captured, a storm carried him and the Arcadian fleet to Cyprus, where he founded Paphos and erected a temple of Aphrodite.

l: Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Agapenor led the Arcadians to Ilium. After its capture, a storm carried Agapenor and the Arcadian fleet away from their intended return voyage.

l: Cyprus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: A storm carried Agapenor and the Arcadian fleet to Cyprus after the capture of Ilium. Agapenor became the founder of Paphos there, and his daughter Laodice later sent a robe from sacred Cyprus to Tegea.

l: Paphos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Agapenor founded Paphos after a storm carried him and the Arcadian fleet to Cyprus. He also erected the temple of Aphrodite in the town.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Hippothous transferred the seat of the Arcadian kingdom from Tegea to Trapezus. Laodice sent a robe from Cyprus to Tegea for Athene Alea, and the Lacedæmonians later invaded the district around Tegea but were defeated by the men of Tegea and by women who took up arms.

l: Æpytus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Æpytus, son of Hippothous, succeeded his father and was blinded after entering the temple of Poseidon at Mantinea, where entry was forbidden; he died soon afterward. Another Æpytus, the sister’s son of Olæas, was restored to Messene by Olæas and the Heraclidæ from Lacedæmon and Argos.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The temple of Poseidon at Mantinea forbade entry both then and later. Æpytus entered it, was struck blind, and died not long afterward.

l: Cypselus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Cypselus was king of Arcadia when the Dorians returned to the Peloponnese by sea. He gave his daughter in marriage to Cresphontes, thereby gaining Cresphontes' support and securing the Arcadians against danger.

l: Lacedæmon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Olæas joined with the Heraclidæ from Lacedæmon and Argos to restore Æpytus to Messene. Aristocrates was later accused of receiving bribes from Lacedæmon and betraying the Messenians.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Lacedæmonians, under Charillus, invaded the district around Tegea but were defeated by the men and women of Tegea. They later fought against the Messenians, while the Arcadians supported the Messenians.

l: Messenia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Æpytus was restored to Messenia by Olæas and the Heraclidæ from Lacedæmon and Argos. The Arcadians supported the Messenians during their war with the Lacedæmonians.

l: Æchmis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Æchmis, son of Briacas and nephew of Polymestor, succeeded Polymestor as king. During his reign the war between the Lacedæmonians and Messenians broke out, and his son Aristocrates acted against the interests of the Arcadians.

l: Aristocrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Aristocrates, son of Æchmis, committed sacrilege by defiling the priestess of Artemis Hymnia at the altar near her statue, and the Arcadians stoned him to death. A later Aristocrates, grandson of Hicetas and bearing the same name, was also stoned to death after accepting bribes from Lacedæmon and betraying the Messenians at the Great Trench.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Artemis Hymnia had a temple on the borders between Orchomenus and Mantinea and was worshipped by all the Arcadians. After Aristocrates defiled her priestess at the altar, the Arcadians changed the priesthood from a maiden to a woman who had withdrawn from the company of men.

l: Great Trench, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Messenians suffered a great reverse at the Great Trench. A later Aristocrates was accused of betraying them there after receiving bribes from Lacedæmon.

l: war between Lacedæmonians and Messenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The war between the Lacedæmonians and Messenians began during the reign of Æchmis. The Arcadians, who had long favored the Messenians, openly fought alongside Aristodemus, king of Messenia.

l: Dorian return to the Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: During the reign of Cypselus, the Dorians returned to the Peloponnese in ships and landed near the Promontory of Rhium. This differed from their earlier attempt, led by Hyllus, which approached by way of the Isthmus of Corinth.

l: Aristocrates' sacrilege, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Aristocrates attempted to seduce the maiden priestess of Artemis Hymnia and defiled her at the altar near the goddess's statue when she fled there for refuge. The Arcadians stoned him to death and thereafter appointed a woman rather than a maiden as priestess.

l: betrayal of the Messenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: A later Aristocrates betrayed the Messenians at the great reverse they suffered at the Great Trench after receiving bribes from Lacedæmon. The Arcadians detected his conduct and stoned him to death.

l: deposition of the descendants of Cypselus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The betrayal of the Messenians by Aristocrates was the reason that all the descendants of Cypselus were deposed from the sovereignty of Arcadia.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Arcadians describe their major historical wars and alliances, including their changing relations with the Lacedæmonians and their membership in the Achæan League. They remained neutral against Philip and the Macedonians and did not fight the Galati at Thermopylæ, according to their own account. The text then describes the passes leading into Arcadia from Argolis, especially those near Mantinea, and identifies nearby water sources, sanctuaries, and rivers.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Arcadians fought against Ilium and alongside the Messenians against the Lacedæmonians, and they took part in the battle of Platæa. They fought under the Lacedæmonians when compelled, but after the Lacedæmonians were defeated at Leuctra they joined the Thebans; they remained neutral against Philip, the Macedonians, and Antipater, and they were among the most zealous members of the Achæan League.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Lacedæmonians fought against the Arcadians and had the Arcadians serve under them against the Athenians and in Agesilaus's expedition to Asia Minor. After their defeat at Leuctra, the Arcadians abandoned them and joined the Thebans; the Arcadians also feared that they would ravage Arcadia if the Arcadian young men went to fight at Thermopylæ.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Arcadia was the land from which the Arcadians came, and it could be entered from Argolis through passes leading toward Tegea and Mantinea. The region included Melangea, which supplied Mantinea with drinking water.

l: Argolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Argolis was connected to Arcadia by passes through Hysiæ, Parthenium, and Mantinea. The Inachus, after leaving the mountain road where it marked the boundary between the Argives and Mantineans, flowed through Argolis and was therefore called the Argive river by Æschylus and others.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Mantinea was approached from Argolis by two passes called Holm-Oak and Ladder, as well as by the narrower pass over Artemisium. Melangea supplied its people with drinking water, and the Inachus marked its boundary with the Argives while it flowed along the mountain road.

l: passes into Arcadia from Argolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The passes into Arcadia from Argolis ran by Hysiæ and across Parthenium toward Tegea, and two others led through Mantinea by Holm-Oak and Ladder. Ladder was the broadest and had steps cut into it; beyond it lay Melangea and, about seven stades farther, the well of the Meliastæ. Another route crossed Artemisium and was much narrower than Ladder-pass.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The district of Mantinea is reached by crossing Artemisium, and its plain Argum is described as unfruitful because rainwater disappears into the ground and later reappears at Dine. Ruins near the plain mark the camp of Philip, son of Amyntas, who came to Arcadia to win over the Arcadians and separate them from the other Greeks. Philip is praised for his military valour but condemned for breaking oaths, violating truces, and dishonouring good faith. His death at the age of forty-six fulfilled a Delphic oracle, and the text connects the early deaths of Alexander and Philip’s family with the end of Macedonian supremacy.

l: district of Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The district of Mantinea is entered by crossing Artemisium. Its plain Argum lies within the district.

l: plain Argum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The plain Argum is called unfruitful because rain from the mountains makes it swampy, though the water disappears into a cavity in the ground and reappears at Dine. A mountain beside it contains ruins of Philip’s camp and of the village Nestane.

l: Philip the son of Amyntas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Philip, son of Amyntas, encamped at Nestane and used Arcadia in an attempt to win over the Arcadians and separate them from the other Greeks. He is regarded as the most valiant of the Macedonian kings, but not as a good man because he broke oaths, violated truces, and dishonoured good faith.

l: Philip’s death, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Philip’s death came when he was forty-six and fulfilled a Delphic oracle that had been given to him when he asked about the Persian war. The oracle’s reference to the crowned bull and the approaching sacrificer was shown to concern Philip himself rather than the Mede.

l: Alexander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Alexander is said to have died early. The text suggests that Philip’s disregard for the principle that a conscientious man’s descendants will prosper left no reason for the gods to preserve Alexander’s life.

l: Macedonian supremacy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The end of Macedonian supremacy is linked with Alexander’s early death. The text suggests that Philip’s conduct and disregard for good faith were connected with the gods ending Alexander’s life and Macedonian supremacy.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The unit describes the traditions, founding, and history of Mantinea. Mantineus is said to have founded it, while Antinoe later led its transfer to another site under the guidance of a serpent, giving the nearby river the name Ophis. Mantinea was conquered and partly destroyed by Agesipolis after he diverted the Ophis through its unbaked-brick walls, but it was later restored by the Thebans. The Mantineans shifted alliances repeatedly, joining the Lacedæmonians, the Achaean League, or other powers at different times, and the city’s name was changed to Antigonea before Adrian restored Mantinea.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Mantinea was founded by Mantineus, the son of Lycaon, and later transferred to its present site by Antinoe, the daughter of Cepheus. Agesipolis captured it by diverting the Ophis through its unbaked-brick walls, leaving part habitable and razing most of it; the Thebans later restored the Mantineans from surrounding villages. The city was renamed Antigonea under Antigonus, but Adrian later restored the name Mantinea.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Arcadians said that Poseidon was raised among flocks and that Rhea deceived Cronos with a foal, and they associated the fountain Arne with the word for lamb. They also regarded Antinoe’s serpent guide as the reason the river beside Mantinea was called Ophis. Most Arcadians supported Antony at Actium, unlike the Mantineans, who supported Augustus.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Lacedæmonians fought against Mantinea at various times. Under King Agesipolis they invaded and captured Mantinea, while later Mantinea made an offensive and defensive alliance with them against the Thebans. Mantinea subsequently became hostile to them, defeated Agis with Achaean assistance, and helped the Achæans weaken their power.

l: Agesipolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Agesipolis, son of Pausanias and king of Sparta, invaded the territory of Mantinea, defeated the Mantineans, and captured their city. He did so by turning the river Ophis through the city walls, causing the unbaked brick to dissolve.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Mantineans joined the Achaean League after becoming at variance with the Lacedæmonians. They defeated Agis in self-defence with an Achaean force under Aratus and later joined the Achæans against Cleomenes, helping to break down the power of the Lacedæmonians.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The unit describes the temples, tombs, monuments, and religious practices of the Mantineans and the city of Mantinea. It mentions temples and statues dedicated to deities including Æsculapius, Leto, Hera, Aphrodite Symmachia, Athene Alea, and Antinous. It recounts the transfer of Arcas’s remains to Mantinea and identifies tombs and monuments associated with Arcas, Gryllus the son of Xenophon, Antinoe, and Podares. It also records Mantinean participation in the seafight off Actium and honors awarded for bravery in the battle against Epaminondas and the Thebans.

l: Mantineans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Mantineans maintain numerous temples and shrines, including those of Zeus, Castor and Pollux, Demeter and Proserpine, Hera, Aphrodite Symmachia, Athene Alea, and Antinous. They keep a fire continually burning in the temple of Demeter and Proserpine, honor Antinous with annual rites and games every fifth year, and erected a temple to Aphrodite Symmachia to commemorate their participation with the Romans in the seafight off Actium. They also honor Arcas and Podares, and say that Gryllus the son of Xenophon was the bravest man in the battle against Epaminondas and the Thebans, followed by Cephisodorus and Podares.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Mantinea contains the temples, monuments, and tombs described in the unit, including the tomb of Arcas near the theatre and a temple of Antinous. It has a Gymnasium room richly decorated with precious stones and paintings, many depicting Antinous, and it contains an imitation of the painting at Ceramicus showing the action of the Athenians at Mantinea.

l: Arcas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Arcas, the son of Callisto, has a tomb near the altar of Hera at Mantinea. His remains were brought from Mænalus to Mantinea in accordance with an oracle at Delphi, and the place of his tomb is called the altars of the Sun.

l: Gryllus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Gryllus the son of Xenophon is represented on a pillar above a tomb near the theatre, carved as a man on horseback. The Mantineans say that he was the bravest of their own men or allies in the battle against Epaminondas and the Thebans.

l: Antinous, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Antinous is regarded as a god at Mantinea, where he has the city’s latest temple and annual rites, with games held every fifth year. The Mantineans honor him because he was born at Bithynium and the Bithynians were originally Arcadians from Mantinea; his images and paintings in the Gymnasium make him resemble young Dionysus.

l: battle of Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: A painting in Mantinea imitates the painting at Ceramicus of the action of the Athenians at Mantinea. The Mantineans also refer to the battle against Epaminondas and the Thebans, in which they say Gryllus the son of Xenophon, Cephisodorus of Marathon, and Podares were the leading examples of bravery.

l: Podares, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Podares has a hero-chapel in the market-place, and the Mantineans say that he fell in the battle against Epaminondas and the Thebans. Three generations before the narrator’s time, they altered the inscription on his tomb to suit a descendant and namesake, but continued to honor the older Podares.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The unit describes notable places on the roads from Mantinea through Arcadia, especially the temple of Poseidon Hippius near the city. It recounts the temple’s ancient construction, the impious entry of Æpytus, and the tradition that seawater springs from within it. It also relates how the Mantineans and other Arcadians defeated the Lacedæmonians and Agis in battle, with Poseidon reportedly helping them. A stone trophy was erected to Poseidon for the victory, and the lineage of Leocydes is connected with an ancient stag tradition.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Arcadia has roads leading from Mantinea to its other parts. In the battle against the Lacedæmonians, the Arcadians held the left wing, with each town under its own commander.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Mantinea has a horseracing place near its walls, a course where games to Antinous take place, and the nearby temple of Poseidon Hippius. Its forces, commanded by Podares, fought on the right wing against the Lacedæmonians, and the Mantineans attributed their victory partly to Poseidon.

l: temple of Poseidon Hippius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The temple of Poseidon Hippius was rebuilt in the writer’s day by the Emperor Adrian, who ordered the new temple to be constructed around the old one and forbade anyone to inspect or disturb the ancient ruins. The older temple was said to have been built by Agamedes and Trophonius, and a woollen thread was once stretched across its entrance. Tradition held that seawater sprang up inside it.

l: Poseidon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Poseidon Hippius was worshipped at the temple near Mantinea. According to the account, he struck Æpytus blind with seawater after Æpytus broke through the thread guarding the temple, and he was said to have appeared to help the Mantineans in battle.

l: stone trophy at Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Mantineans erected a stone trophy after their victory over the Lacedæmonians and Agis. They said it was a votive offering to Poseidon because he had appeared to help them.

l: battle of Mantinea against the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: In the battle, the Mantineans held the right wing, the other Arcadians the left, and Aratus with the Sicyonians and Achæans the centre. Aratus deliberately fell back in a crescent formation, allowing the Arcadians to attack the Lacedæmonians’ flanks; the Lacedæmonians were surrounded, lost most of their men, and Agis fell.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Lacedæmonians extended their battle line to avoid being outflanked, with Agis and his staff in the centre. They pressed Aratus’s division fiercely, but after Aratus withdrew and the Arcadians attacked their flanks, they were surrounded and suffered heavy losses.

l: Agis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Agis commanded the Lacedæmonians and occupied the centre with his staff. He pressed hard against Aratus’s division but was surrounded with his army and fell in the battle.

l: Poseidon’s intervention in the battle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Mantineans said that Poseidon appeared and helped them defeat the Lacedæmonians and Agis. The account considers that the victory may have been largely due to Poseidon, comparing it with traditions of divine beings assisting in other battles.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The unit describes places near Mantinea, including Pelagos, the tombs of the daughters of Pelias, and the supposed tomb of Areithous. It recounts the battle at Mantinea, where Epaminondas was mortally wounded and later died, with Mantinean, Spartan, Athenian, and Theban accounts differing about who wounded him. It also explains how an oracle at Delphi misled Epaminondas through the ambiguous name Pelagos, and compares this with the misleading place-names in the stories of Hannibal the Carthaginian and the Athenians.

l: Pelagos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Pelagos is an oak plantation near the temple of Poseidon, along the road from Mantinea to Tegea and later along the road from Mantinea to Pallantium. The boundary between Mantinea and Tegea is marked by a round altar on the highroad, and the cavalry of the Mantineans and Athenians fought the Bœotian cavalry at Pelagos.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Mantinea has roads leading to Tegea and Pallantium through or alongside the oak plantation called Pelagos. Its people say that the daughters of Pelias lived there after their father’s death, that Machærion killed Epaminondas, and that Gryllus received a public funeral and statue for his bravery.

l: daughters of Pelias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The daughters of Pelias were deceived by Medea into helping to cut up and boil their father in the hope of making him young again. They were left with hardly enough of Pelias to bury and went to live in Arcadia, where they later died and received tombs; Mico identified them as Asteropea and Antinoe.

l: Medea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Medea plotted against Pelias for Jason’s interest while pretending to be hostile to him. She demonstrated that she could restore youth by boiling an old ram with herbs, then persuaded the daughters of Pelias to cut up and boil their father, who was not restored.

l: Pelias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Pelias was targeted by Medea after she came to Iolcos. His daughters cut him up and boiled him at Medea’s direction, but they obtained hardly enough of him to provide a burial.

l: battle at Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: At the battle at Mantinea, the cavalry of the Mantineans and Athenians fought the Bœotian cavalry. Epaminondas was mortally wounded during the battle, and differing accounts name Machærion or Gryllus as the person who wounded him.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Epaminondas was mortally wounded at the battle at Mantinea and was carried alive from the fighting. He watched the battle while holding his wound, then died after the battle and was buried on the field, where a pillar, a shield bearing a dragon, and two other pillars commemorated him; he is praised as a Greek general of exceptional talent who raised the Thebans to a foremost position.

l: Gryllus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: According to the Athenians, with the Thebans supporting their account, Gryllus mortally wounded Epaminondas. The Mantineans gave Gryllus a public funeral and erected his statue on a pillar where he fell, honoring him as the bravest man in the allied army.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Athenians fought alongside the Mantineans against the Bœotian cavalry at Pelagos. Their account, corroborated by the Thebans, says that Gryllus mortally wounded Epaminondas; they also misunderstood an oracle about colonizing Sicily and undertook the fatal war against Syracuse.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Thebans supported the Athenian account that Gryllus mortally wounded Epaminondas. Epaminondas is credited with transforming the Thebans from a people accustomed to obeying other Greek states into a foremost power.

l: oracle at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
