s: The oracle at Delphi warned Epaminondas to beware of Pelagos. He understood Pelagos to mean the sea and avoided traveling on a trireme or transport, but Apollo evidently meant the oak plantation near Mantinea.

l: Hannibal the Carthaginian, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Hannibal the Carthaginian received an oracle from Ammon saying that he would die and be buried in Libyssa. He expected this to refer to Libya, but he died from a fever after wounding his finger, at a place near Nicomedia that was called Libyssa.

l: Sicily, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Sicily was the subject of an oracle telling the Athenians to colonize it. The Athenians failed to recognize that the oracle referred to a small hill called Sicily near Athens and instead went beyond their borders, leading to the fatal war against Syracuse.

l: oracles and ambiguous place-names, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The unit presents several cases in which people misunderstood an oracle because a place-name had more than one possible reference. Epaminondas interpreted Pelagos as the sea, Hannibal interpreted Libyssa as Libya, and the Athenians interpreted Sicily as the distant island rather than the small hill near Athens.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Near Mantinea are the temple of Zeus Charmo, the plain of Alcimedon, and the boundary with Megalopolis. Alcimedon, one of the Heroes, lived in a cave on Mount Ostracina, where Hercules rescued Alcimedon's daughter Phialo and her exposed infant son. Two roads lead from Mantinea to Orchomenus, passing the alleged tomb of Penelope, the ruins of old Mantinea, and the well of Alalcomenea. Another road to Orchomenus passes Mount Anchisia and the tomb of Anchises, who was said to have died and been buried there.

l: Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Mantinea has roads leading to the village of Methydrium and to Orchomenus. Near one road are the ruins of old Mantinea, a place still called The Town, and the boundary between Mantinea and Orchomenus is at Mount Anchisia; Petrosaca marks its boundary with Megalopolis.

l: Alcimedon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Alcimedon was one of the men called Heroes and lived in a cave on Mount Ostracina above the plain called Alcimedon. When his daughter Phialo became a mother, he exposed her and her newborn boy on the mountain.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: According to the tradition of the Phigalians, Hercules had an intrigue with Phialo, the daughter of Alcimedon. Hearing a jay imitate the exposed boy's cries, Hercules found Phialo, loosed her from her bonds, and saved the boy's life.

l: Phialo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Phialo was the daughter of Alcimedon and had an intrigue with Hercules. After Alcimedon discovered that she had become a mother, he exposed her and her newborn son, but Hercules later released and saved her.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Two roads lead from Mantinea to Orchomenus. One passes Ladas' course, a temple of Artemis, the alleged tomb of Penelope, the well of Alalcomenea, and the ruins of Mæra; another passes Mount Anchisia, whose district boundary separates Orchomenus from Mantinea.

l: tomb of Penelope, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: A lofty mound near one of the roads from Mantinea to Orchomenus is said to be the tomb of Penelope. It stands near a small plain and the ruins of old Mantinea, a place still called The Town.

l: Penelope, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Thesprotian Poem represents Penelope as bearing Ptoliporthes to Odysseus after his return from Troy. The Mantineans instead say that Odysseus discovered her encouraging the suitors, sent her away, and that she went first to Lacedæmon, then to Mantinea, where she died.

l: Odysseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: According to the Mantinean tradition, Odysseus discovered that Penelope had encouraged the suitors to his house and sent her away. The Thesprotian Poem instead represents him as the father of Penelope's son Ptoliporthes after his return from Troy.

l: Anchises, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Anchises was said to have come to the place at the foot of Mount Anchisia, died there, and been buried there. The mountain was named Anchisia after him, and ruins of a temple of Aphrodite stand near his tomb.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The unit describes Orchomenus, including its ancient hilltop walls and marketplace, its later settlement, local water source, temples, Artemis statue, and unidentified war tombs. It explains the distinctive lifelong separation of the priestess and priest of Hymnian Artemis and mentions the goddess’s annual festival. The surrounding landscape includes Mount Trachys, a marshy plain, roads to Caphya, Stymphelus, and Pheneus, and the tomb of Aristocrates, who violated the priestess of Artemis Hymnia. It also identifies Amilus, formerly a town, and Caryæ at the end of a ravine leading toward Pheneus.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Orchomenus had an old town on a hill, with surviving ruins of its walls and marketplace, while the contemporary town lay within the old circuit. It had a well, temples of Poseidon and Aphrodite with stone statues, and a wooden statue of Artemis in a cedar tree. Its territory included a small marshy plain and roads leading toward Caphya, Stymphelus, and Pheneus.

l: Hymnian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Hymnian Artemis was worshipped by Orchomenus and Mantinea. Her priestess and priest remained separate from one another throughout their lives, sharing neither marriage, baths, meals, nor visits to strangers’ houses. She also received an annual festival, and Aristocrates was said to have violated her priestess.

l: Mount Trachys, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Mount Trachys stood opposite Orchomenus. Rainwater passed through a hollow ravine between the town and the mountain before descending into another plain belonging to Orchomenus.

l: Caphya, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Caphya was reached from Orchomenus by a straight road running beside the ravine and marsh. Its territory shared a mountain boundary with Orchomenus and Pheneus, near the Caphyatic rock and a ravine leading to Pheneus.

l: tomb of Aristocrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The tomb of Aristocrates stood on the road from Orchomenus toward Pheneus, after the road passed beneath Mount Trachys. The wells called Teneæ were next to it.

l: Aristocrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Aristocrates violated the priestess of Artemis Hymnia. His tomb stood on the road from Orchomenus toward Pheneus, beside the wells called Teneæ.

l: Amilus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Amilus was a place about seven stades beyond the wells called Teneæ. The people said that it had formerly been a town, and the road there branched toward Stymphelus and Pheneus.

l: Pheneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pheneus was reached by a road branching near Amilus and passing through a ravine. Its territory shared a mountain boundary with Orchomenus and Caphya, and Caryæ lay at the end of the ravine leading toward it.

l: Caryæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Caryæ was a town situated at the end of the ravine on the road leading toward Pheneus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Pheneus lies below Caryæ and was said to have been destroyed by a deluge, with water pits and a canal associated with Hercules. The people of Pheneus attributed their founding to the autochthon Pheneus and preserved traditions about Odysseus, including his horses, a temple to Artemis Heurippe, and a statue of Poseidon Hippius. The unit also describes the tomb and hero-cult of Iphicles, the worship of Hermes, and the tomb and annual nighttime honors of Myrtilus. Pausanias questions whether the bronze statue of Poseidon could really have been an offering of Odysseus and rejects the claim that the Myrtoan Sea was named after Myrtilus.

l: Pheneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Pheneus lies below Caryæ, and the old Pheneus was said to have been destroyed by a deluge. Hercules was said to have lived there, dug a channel for the river Olbius, and made pits to receive water from the plain; the river later abandoned his canal. Pheneus had a precipitous citadel with a partly fortified area, a ruined temple of Athene Tritonia, the tomb of Iphicles, a temple of Hermes, and the tomb of Myrtilus.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Hercules was said to have lived at Pheneus with Laonome, the mother of Amphitryon, and may have gone there after being expelled from Tiryns by Eurystheus. He dug pits at the mountains Oryxis and Sciathis and a channel through the plain for the river Olbius, though the river later returned to its old channel.

l: people of Pheneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The people of Pheneus said that the pits near their plain were made by Hercules and that Pheneus, an autochthon, was their founder. They preserved traditions that Odysseus found his lost horses there and that Myrtilus was buried there, and they paid heroic honors to Iphicles and annual nighttime honors to Myrtilus. They especially honored Hermes and held games called Hermæa.
